ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Report of the S.L. Kapoor Committee on Credit to SSI 
*201. SHRI CR THIR UNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Committee on Credit to Small Scale Sector under the 
chairmanship of Shri S.L. Kapur has submitted its report to Government; 
(b) if so, the details of the main recommendations; 
(c) whether Government have examined the report; 
(d) if so, action proposed to be taken by Government thereon; and 
(e) the other measures proposed to be taken by which S.S.I, funds reach 
the grassroot level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had in December, 1997 appointed a One 
Man Committee headed by Shri S.L. Kapur, the then Member, Board for 
Industrial & Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to review inter-alia (i) the working 
of credit delivery system of small scale industries with a view to making the 
system more effective, simple and effi cient to administer and (ii) to make 
suggestions for simplification and improvements in systems and procedures. 
The Committee submitted its report to RBI on 30th June, 1998 which contains 
126 recommendations. Out of 126 recommendations, 103 have been examined by 
the RBI and decision taken thereon. Banks/Financial Institutions and other 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001 ] 
agencies have already implemented 86 recommendations. Some of the important 
measures taken pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee include: 
(0  De-linking of SIDBI from IDBI. 
(ii)  Opening of more specialized Branches. 
(iii) Enhancement in the limits of Composite Loan from Rs. 2 lakhs to Rs. 
5 lakhs. 
(iv)   Setting up of more DRTs. 
(v)  Introduction of Credit Guarantee Scheme. 
(vi) Raising the exemption limit for collateral security from Rs. 25,000 to 
Rs. 5 lakhs. 
Seventeen Recommendations have not been found feasible for acceptable 
at this stage. However, review of policies and procedures is a continuous exercise. 
Remaining 23 recommendations are under examination at various stages. Other 
measures taken by Government and RBI for promotion and development of 
Small Scale Industry inter-alia include the following: 
(i) RBI advised banks to follow the procedure of sanctioning working 
capital limits computed on the basis of minimum of 20% of the 
projected annual turnover to all SSI Units requiring aggregate fund 
based working capital limits upto Rs. 5 crores 
(ii) RBI Advised banks to ensure that out of their total fundsient to SSI 
Sector, at least 40% should be made available to units with investment 
in Plant & Machinery upto Rs. 5 lakhs and 20% should be made 
available to units with investment in plant and machinery between 
Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 25 lakhs. 
(iii) Increased the Project Cost Limit under National Equity Fund (NEF) 
Scheme from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 25 lakh (Union Budget 2000-2001) 
and further to Rs. 50 lakh. Like-wise Soft Loan component on NEF 
has also been raised to Rs. 10 lakhs. 
(iv) RBI advised Banks to fix sub-limits within overall limit to the large 
borrowers specifically for meeting the payment obligations in respect 
of purchases from SSI. 
2

(v) Introduced Credit Linked Capital Subsidy for the upgradation of the 
Small Scale Industries. 
(vi) Enhanced limits of Composite Loan to Rs. 25 lakhs, and raised 
exemption limit for collateral security to Rs. 5 lakhs. 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Sir, the Government of India's policy on 
small-scale industries has always been ad hoc, piecemeal and problem-solving. The 
problem that is being faced  by the small-scale industr ies is finance, industrial 
sickness and technological backwardness. More than two lakh small-scale units are 
sick. Till today, we are not able to ascertain the reasons for the same. The various 
financial schemes announced by the Government are only ♦ on paper, meaningless 
and are not being implemented. These schemes are not going to the root of the 
problem. Shri K.C. Pant, the Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission, has 
said, I am glad to inform you that the proposed set up Credit Guarantee Fund, with 
the contribution of the Government of India, SIDBI, in the ratio of 4:1, to provide 
75 per cent of credit guarantee to loans up to Rs. 10 lakhs to small-scale units is 
under active consideration. But the Report of S.L. Kapur, which was placed on the 
Table of the House on 12th June, 2001, states, though announcement of Credit 
Guarantee Scheme in August last year was a step in the right direction, the available 
statistics show that it has not succeeded  in reaching the sufficient number of SSI 
units...—he further noted— ...That only 1,276 projects have been accorded 
approval for guarantee cover before end of 2nd of Apri 1,2001. There is a call for 
synergy between the commercial banks and the SIDBI to promote it at the grass-root 
level. The loan limit, under the scheme, up to Rs. 25 lakh borrowers, is 75 per cent of 
the renewals; availability of loan is up to Rs. 1 lakh only. Though the eligib ility of 
loan limit has been enhanced to Rs. 25 lakhs, they are getting only Rs. 1 lakh as loan. I 
want to know from the hon. Minister whether it is not true that the statement of Shri 
K.C. Pant contradicts the statement of Sh ri S.L. Kapur, on credit guarantee. I also 
want to know from the hon. Minister whether the Credit Guarantee Scheme 
announced for the SSI is functioning properly; and, if so, how many applications have 
so far been proposed and cleared. I would also like to know as  to what steps the 
Ministry has taken to speed up the Credit Guarantee Scheme to bring light in the life 
of the small-scale units. 
 Sir, I say it with great respect that in China, the small-scale units are 
flourishing, but in India they are perishing, I want to know as to what is the reason.

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL: Sir, as far as the sickness is concerned, 
the hon. Member has said that more than two lakh units are sick. But, now as per 
the figures of August, 2000, the total number of small-scale units is 32 lakhs; and 
the total number of sick units is about 54,000. 
With regard to the Credit Guarantee Scheme, I would like to submit that 
we have started it recently and it is yet to take off. But it is true that some banks 
are not co-operating with the applicants. So, we are monitoring it. At the same 
time a number of other measures for improvement of the SSIs are also taken. 
We are taking steps with regard to the Credit Guarantee Scheme etc. The 
hon. Prime Minister had announced a pa ckage; I hope the hon. Member is 
fully aware of that. At the same time, the Ministry has increased the working 
capital limit from Rs. 2 crores to Rs. 4 crores then to Rs. 5 crores; excise duty 
exemption also has been increased from Rs. 30 lakhs to Rs. 1 crore. So, we 
have taken a number of measures... 
SHRI CR THIRUNAVUKKA RASU: Sir, my question is how many 
applications the Ministry has processed. 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL: I will collect the information... 
SHRI CR THIRUNAVUKKARASU: How many applications the 
Ministry has processed subsequent to that? That is my question. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): Sir, the 
Credit 
Guarantee Scheme, which was a very courageous step taken by the Government 
was started with effect from 1st August, 2000. So far, 24 eligible lending 
institutions have been registered for this purpose. The eligible loan limit for 
coverage under the scheme has been enhanced to Rs. 25 lakhs, as the hon. 
Member has mentioned. At the end of October, 2001, a total number of 
2,143 cases have been approved by th e trust, extending guarantee cover for 
aggregate loan of Rs. 1,633 lakhs. This is the figure. So, it is not correct to say 
that  scheme has not taken off. Within a short span of little over one year, the 
scheme has taken off; applications ar e being received. As my colleague has 
just mentioned, reviewing the functioning of the credit flow to the SSI sector is 
a permanent item on our agenda. We meet with the bank chiefs once in six 
months. We had a meeting in July this year, where we had specially invited 
the Minister of SSI to attend the meeting. There, we discussed in detail the 
financing for the SSI sector. In November, I held another meeting with the bank 
chiefs, where again, this was  a special item on the agenda. So, we are 
continuously reviewing the flow of credit to the SSI sector, exactly in order 
to take care of the concern of the hon.

Member. The schemes that we have repeatedly announced over the years are 
not merely confined to the paper, they are actually implemented on the ground. 
SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Due to the emergence of the WTO 
and global marketing in the world, what will be the impact and the implications 
on the small-scale industries in India? Will it be helpful or will it have an 
adverse effect? 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is a fact that due 
to the WTO and opening up of the economy, impact on the SSI is there. But, at 
the same time, we are seeing that the dumping of the material should not be 
here. By imposing the antidumping duty and increasing custom duties, the SSI 
is given protection. At the same time, we are trying to boost the exports from the 
SSI sector. We are giving a number of other schemes for technology upgradation, 
and also some interest concessions on those items. Of course, there is definitely 
a fear amongst the SSI community that th is impact will be there. But we are 
having various measures, delinking of the SIDBI, total subsidy for technical 
upgradation. That way, we are trying to give a new strategy. At the same time, 
the industry is not happy even afte r the package announced by the Prime 
Minister. But in totality, Sir, the growth rate of the SSI is far better than the 
overall industrial growth. The industrial growth rate is 4.9 per cent; but the SSI 
growth rate is 8.1 per cent. The growth rate of large industries is 2.6 or 2.7 per 
cent. So, the total growth rate of the SSI is far better. As far as employment is 
concerned, I can give you the figures as of today. The total employment is more 
than 6 per cent, but there is no retrenchment. There are some sick units also. The 
Government has announced a number of schemes for the sick units which have 
the potential to become viable. The industry is slowly coming out that way. 
The performance during the last quarter  has been very attractive than the 
previous one. 
SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: My question was whether there was 
any impact of the WTO and globalisation on the SSI. (Interruptions)

large amount of non-performing assets. Therefore, they are not able to perform 
their traditional functions of lending to small and medium industries. I believe,

State Finance Corporations are not delivering the goods. May I give some figures

yet to come. The State Financial Corporations are not working up to the mark. 
Today, it is as good as nonfunctional. 
SHRI ARJUN SINGH: Sir, what does this mean? We are totally at a loss to

SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, may I supplement the answer given by 
my colleague? Sir, the hon. Leader of the Opposition is quite right in saying 
that we had a number of committees which had gone into the functioning of 
the State Finance Corporations. Like many institutions in the financial sector, 
as my colleague had just pointed out,  the State Finance Corporations have 
also run into major problems, because  the NPAs have expanded. Now, the 
question, basically, in regard to the revival of the State Finance Corporations, 
is of recapitalisation. Suggestions have been made with regard to 
recapitalisation of SFCs. This is a matter which we are discussing with the 
State Governments and I am hopeful that we would be able to resolve this

Statement 
(a) to (d) Commercial reserves of hydrocarbons have not yet been 
established in the State of Uttar Pradesh. 
However, in order to accelerate pace of exploration efforts in the country. 
Government approved in February, 1997, a New Exploration Licensing Policy 
(NELP) providing a number of attractive fiscal and contractual terms to the 
bidders, from both public and private sectors, to participate in the activities of 
exploration of hydrocarbons. Under this Policy, companies have the freedom 
to market the oil and gas produced fr om the contract area in the domestic 
market. Blocks GV-ONN-97/1 and GV-ONN-2000/1 in the State of Uttar Pradesh 
covering areas of 36,750 sq. km. and 23,500 sq. km. respectively were awarded 
to the consortium of Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. and Indian Oil 
Corporation Ltd. (ONGC-IOC) under the first round and second round of NELP 
respectively.

Growth rate of per capita income 
204. SHRI JIBON ROY : Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state the rate of growth of per capita income during 1996-97 to 2000-01 
(financial year-wise) at constant 1993-94 price? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA) : A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The rate of growth of per capita income during 1996-97, 1997-98, 1998-
99,1999-2000 and 2000-01 (financial year wise) at constant (1993-94) prices, is 
6.3 per cent, 2.8 per cent, 4.8 per cent, 4.8 per cent and 3.5 per cent respectively. 
SHRI JIBON ROY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the fugures given by the hon. 
Minister indicate that the decline in the economy is not a recent phenomenon. 
20 
 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The growth rate of per capita income has gone down from 6.3 per cent in 
1996-97 to 3.5 per cent in 2000-2001, and the decline is much more in the 
current financial year. It indicates that it is not directly linked to the 
international slow-down alone. Something else is there. It is being written, 
nowadays, by many economists that it is the consequence of a jobless growth. 
Initially, when the economy was integrated with globalisation, there was a 
boom in the market. Now there is a demand constraint. Would the hon. Minister 
agree that because of demand constraint the economy is declining? What steps 
has the Government taken to meet the expenditure demand of the people? 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, it is nobody's case and certainly not 
the Government's case that the slow down that the Indian economy is 
experiencing is entirely on account of the external environment. It is also 
not the Government's case that it is of recent origin; that it is linked to the 
11th September. That has never been the stand that the Government has 
taken. The Government is aware of the fact that there is slowdown in the 
Indian economy. I have already explained about the slowdown in the Indian 
economy. I had stood in this House and explained that there were some 
external reasons for the slowdown. The external reason, as I had mentioned 
in this House on a previous occasion,  is the collapse of the technology 
stocks in the USA which impacted on our technology sector also. It is because 
of the increase in the international oil prices which went up by almost 300 
per cent starting from 1999 and throughout 2000—until the prices softened 
recently that we had to raise the co nsumer price of petroleum products 
which had an impact on the growth of consumption. In fact, the consumption, 
except in the month of October when it had picked up, has gone down. 
Diesel consumption has actually declined. So, these are the global factors. 
The most important factor which br ought the Indian economy into the 
slowdown phase, I have repeatedly said, is the slowdown in the Indian 
agriculture over the last two years, i.e. 1999-2000 when the contribution of 
agriculture to the GDP declined considerably as compared to the previous 
year. I had also stated in this House that because something like 70 per cent 
of our people live in rural areas and depend on agriculture and allied sectors, 
there has been a contraction of demand. As a result, their purchasing power 
is going down. This is the major domestic reason why there is a slowdown in 
demand. Because of various other facts including the slowdown in demand, 
investment has also slowed down. These are the reasons for the slowdown of 
the Indian economy. The hon. Member is quite right in quoting the figures 
which I have given. But I would like to remind him that while it was 6.3 per 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
cent, in 1996-97, it was 7.8 per cent which was the highest growth rate that 
we have seen in recent years. That was the growth rate of GDP. Therefore, 
the per capita income is 6.3 per cent. That was the growth rate. But if you 
see the next year, 1997-98, it came down to something like 2.8 per cent and 
3.5 per cent is certainly better than 2.8 per cent. It came down to 2.8 per 
cent in 1997-98 for the simple reason that the growth of the Indian economy 
declined from a high of 7.8 per cent in 1996-97 to 4.8 per cent in 1997-98. 
So the growth rate had an impact on the per capita income. That is the 
reason why per capita income has declined. Nobody is under any illusion. I 
would like to disabuse the mind of the hon. Member that it is certainly not 
the Government's case that it is because of the global slowdown that the 
Indian economy has slowed down. It had its impact. The last part of the 
decade 90s has been exceptional in terms of international crisis starting with 
the East Asian crisis. But, as a result of the policies which have been followed 
by the successive Governments, we have been fairly insulated from the impact 
of those international crisis. Even today there is a crisis in turkey. There is 
a crisis in Argentina. We are much better as compared to these countries. 
SHRI JIBON ROY: What remedial  measures have you taken? 
(Interruptions). Despite all constraints, China's growth rate is 7.5 per cent. 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA : I had said, when I presented the Budget,

Therefore, in the Budget, we took two very important steps. We decided to 
soften the interest rate; create a situation which will lead to softening of 
interest rate, and, secondly, across the board, we reduced the taxes, instead 
of increasing them. When I presented the Budget on 20th February this 
year, everyone. ...(Interruptions) 
SHRI JIBON ROY: Softening of interest rates did not help the economy. 
The economy has collapsed; the agricultural economy is in a very bad shape 
in all the States.... 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA : Sir, I have already gone on record to say 
that interest rate reduction alone is not a sufficient factor for fresh investment. 
We will have to create...(Interruptions). 
SHRI JIBON ROY : It became counter-productive... 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA : It is not counter-productive. It is one of 
the various factors which will.help investment. Softening of interest rate 
will help the entrepreneurs to take investment decision; this is one of the 
22 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
various factors. But I agree with the hon. Member that the expansion of 
demand in the domestic economy is the most important factor which will 
lead to expansion in investment as well. And we are hoping that because 
agriculture this year is doing better than in the previous two years, this will 
generate demand in the Indian economy and it will provide the necessary 
fillip to the growth of the Indian economy.

Take over of Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE) by SBI 
*216. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Bank of India has been permitted to tak; over the 
management of the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE); 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
(b) whether it is a fact that the banking industry is on the verge of 
failure in domestic field; and 
(c) if so, whether all pros and cons have been duly considered before 
taking over the management of CBE? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (c) State Bank of India (SBI) has reported 
that it had participated in a global bid floated by Commercial Bank of Ethiopia 
(CBE) for management contract of CBE and SBI's bid was accepted. SBI has 
further reported that certain terms of the specific contract in this regard are still 
under negotiation and the arrangement has not yet been finalised. SBI shall 
seek the approval of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) after negotiation of various 
terms of the contract are concluded. SBI had carried out a detailed due diligence 
exercise and all pros and cons of the arrangement have been duly considered. 
(b) RBI has reported that out of the 100 Scheduled Commercial Banks 
(SCBs) in India, the Capital to Risk Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 95 banks, for the year 
ended 31.3.2001, was more than the minimum stipulation of 9%. The ratio of 
gross non-performing assets to gross advances of the SCBs had improved from 
14.4% in March, 1998 to 11.4% in March, 2001. The operating profits of SCBs 
increased by 7.9% during the year ended 31st March, 2001. Thus, the Indian 
Banking Industry is not on the verge of failure in domestic field. 
Changes in Credit Policy 
*217. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has lately announced drastic 
changes in the credit policy for Banks, reducing the bench mark Bank-rates 
to a 28 years low of 6.5 per cent and slashing the Cash Reserve Ratio from 
7.5 per cent to 5.5. per cent; 
(b) the reasons warranting such changes in the credit policy; 
(c) whether it affects the already poor incentives for the common 
depositors, the workers, the aged and the pensioners to deposit their savings 
in banks; and 
(d) how far the new credit policy is pro-corporate and anti-common 
depositors, the workers, the aged and the pensioners? 
42 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) On a review of macroeconomic and 
monetary developments, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reduced Bank Rate 
by 0.5 percentage point from 7.0 per cent to 6.50 per cent with effect from the 
close of business on October 22,2001 as a part of monetary policy measures 
which are announced six monthly. At this level, it is the lowest Bank Rate since 
May 1973. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was also reduced by 200 basis points to 
5.50 per cent from 7.50 per cent of Net Demand and Time Liabilities 
(NDTL).  
(b) All scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional Rural Banks) 
were required to maintain with the RBI a CRR of 7.5 per cent of their NDTL 
prior to announcement of the mid-term review. While the statutory minimum 
requirement of CRR maintenance at 3.0 per cent is obligatory on the banks 
additional CRR, ranging between 4.5 per cent and 12.0 per cent since 1981, 
was imposed from time to time in order to reduce the overflow of liquidity 
due to excessive money supply in the economy. With a view to rationalizing 
CRR prescription and moving towards the long term goal of keeping CRR 
normally at the statutory level, changes were made in respect of the coverage 
as well as the level of CRR for the banking system. 
It is expected that the recent changes in policy with regard to CRR 
will facilitate the development of a short term yield curve, develop money 
market, reduce the regulatory arbitrage between banks and non-banks, 
enhance the availability of lendable resources with the banks and improve 
the efficiency of indirect instruments in the conduct of monetary policy. 
(c) and (d) The commercial banks are free to determine their interest 
rate structure on bank deposits excepting savings bank accounts, keeping in 
view their own asset liability structure. In addition, banks are permitted to 
formulate fixed deposit schemes specifically meant for senior citizens offering 
higher and fixed rates of interest as compared to normal deposits of any 
size. 
The changes in interest rates are in consonance with the decline in 
inflation and as such are not expected to affect the interest of common 
depositors adversely. .

De-reservation of vacancies for SCs/STs/OBCs 
*219. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a large number of vacancies/posts reserved for SCs/ STs and 
OBCs are being "de-reserved" and filled by "others" despite imposition of ban 
on "de-reservation" of vacancies with effect from 1st April, 1989, by DOPT 
OM No.36012/6/88-Estt. (SCT) dated 25th April, 1989; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the instances where vacancies/posts reserved for SCs/STs and OBCs 
have been de-reserved and filled by persons other than those for whom they 
were reserved since 1st April, 1989 in the Ministry of Finance and its attached 
and subordinate offices during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) The Office Memorandum of the 
Department of Personnel & Training dated 25.4.1989, relating to ban on de-
reservation in direct recruitment to vacancies under the Central Government, 
44 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
also provides that in case of direct recruitment to vacancies in Group A 
Services, there may be rare and exceptional cases where after the non-
availability of suitable SC and/or ST candidates, posts cannot be allowed to 
remain vacant in public interest. In such situations, the adminsitrative 
Ministry/ Department under which the recruitment is being made shall make 
a proposal for dereservation giving full justification for such action, and 
consult the Commissioner for Spheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and 
obtain his comments on each proposal. After obtaining the comments of the 
Commissioner for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, the adminstrative 
Ministry shall then place the propo sal for dereservation along with the 
Commissioner's comments before a Committee comprising the Secretaries 
in the Ministry of Personnel, in the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment 
and the Ministry/ Department under which the recruitment is being made for 
consideration and recommendation. The recommendation of this Committee shall 
be placed before the Minister in charge of the Ministry of Personnel for a final 
decision. In regard to OBCs, the instructions of the Department of Personnel & 
Training provide that the vacancies reserved for OBCs which remain unfilled 
should not be the-reserved but should be carried forward as such for a period of 
three recruitment years or till the vacancies are filled by OBC candidates, 
whichever is earlier. The exact details as to dereservation, if any, in case of 
various offices under the Ministry of Finance are not centrally maintained.

RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Water 
being a State subject, the responsibility of survey and investigation, 
planning, development funding, execution and management of all types of 
water resources projects including flood control and drainage to harness 
the water resources within the States rests with the concerned State 
Government according to their own priorities and from their own plan 
resources. The National Water Policy inter-alia envisages augmenting 
the availability of water by adopting measures for maximizing retention and 
minimizing losses, recharging ground water, a dopting water harvesting 
practices, making water available to water short areas by inter-basin 
transfer based on a national perspective and recycling and re-use of 
water. 
India receives a rainfall of about 4000 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) 
including snowfall every year. As per the latest assessment made by the 
Central Water Commission, the average annual flow in the river systems of 
India is about 1869 BCM. However, due to topographical and environmental 
constraints, natural evaporation and vegetation losses the utilisable surface 
water resources by conventional methods has been assessed as 690 BCM. 
For storage of rain water, about 3600 large dams and reservoirs and 250 
barrages have been constructed in the country. Through these dams, a total 
live storage capacity of 177 BCM has been created upto 1995. An additional 
live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the dams, 
which are under various stages of construction. Proposals to take up additional 
dams to create a live storage capacity of 132 BCM are also under formulation/ 
consideration. The live storage capacity and the percentage of storage capacity 
being stored at present in each State is given in the statement, (see below) 
Besides, about 2,53,000 Tanks (minor dams) and ponds have also been created 
in the country. The replenishable ground water resources are of the order of 
432 BCM out of which about 154 BCM has been developed for use. 
Government of India is also promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water 
and roof-top rainwater harvesting unde r the sector reform project of 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural 
Development, for which technical and Financial assistance is provided 
to the State Government and other implementing agencies. Central Ground 
Water Board has also taken up pilot studi es for artificial ground water 
recharge.

Growth rate of the economy 
†1598. SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that now India is not among one of the two 
fastest developing economies; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
122 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is also a tact that as per the report of the IMF the growth rate is 
likely to fall by 4.5— 5 per cent; 
(c) whether according to the report the growth rate of India is very low as 
compared to the required rate to remove the poverty; and 
(d) if so, the details of the effective measures taken to spur the falling growth 
rate on the track along with the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) As per the World Economic Outlook (WEO) 
October 2001, published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) the real growth in 
India's Gross Domestic Product (GDF) is projected at 4.5 per cent for 2001 or 5 per 
cent for the financial year 2001-02. These October 2001 WEO projections were made 
before the September 11 terrorist attacks. In view of those events, and more recent 
data suggesting that the global economic situation before the attacks was weaker than 
earlier projected, the IMF has revised down its baseline projections for global 
growth. Given that India is less exposed to global developments the growth in 
calendar year 2001 in India is now projected by the IMF to be 4.4 per cent (or 
4.7% in fiscal year 2001-02). Under the revised projections released by the IMF on 
November 13,2001, India is one of the three fastest growing large economies in the 
world, the other two are China and Russia which are expected to grow by 7.3 per 
cent and 5.8 per cent respectively in 2001. It may be noted that Reserve Bank of 
India in its Mid Term Review of Monetary and Credit Policy has placed its 
projection of GDP growth for 2001-02 in the range of 5.0 per cent to 6.0 per cent for 
the Indian economy, the WEO October, 2001 notes that aGDP growth rate of 4.5 per 
cent in India is well below levels considered necessary to make significant inroads 
into poverty. However, WEO does acknowledge that over the last three decades, 
India's poverty rate has declined significantly. 
(d) The Budget for 2001-2002 has provided enhanced central plan outlays for 
key infrastructure sectors and increased emphasis has been placed on accelerating 
capital investment expenditure. Besides, Reserve Bank of India on the basis of a 
review of macro-economic and monetary developments took certain monetary 
measures keeping in view need for adequate liquidity to meet credit growth and 
support revival of investment demand consistent with price stability. These 
measures included further reduction in the bank 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
rate from 7 per cent to 6.5 per cent, rationalization and reduction in the Cash 
Reserve Ratio for the banking system and reduction in the maximum interest rate 
chargeable on export credit by 1.0 percentage point for a period of six months 
with effect from September 26,2001. These specific measures to stimulate 
demand in the backdrop of budget strategy are expected to have a favourable 
impact on growth.

Statutory Powers to River Board Organisations 
1664. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Statutory powers for River Board Organisations in the 
management of water resources have been opposed by certain State 
Governments; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) National 
Water Resources Council (NWRC) while deliberating the draft revised National 
Water Policy in its 4th Meeting held on 7th July, 2000 considered inter alia the 
provision relating to setting up of River Basin Organisations (RBOs) with 
statutory powers. Some of the States like Goa, Himachal Pradesh Kerala, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh had opposed the setting up of 
RBOs with statutory powers. In view of the divergent views expressed on this 
provision relating to RBOs and other provisions of the draft revised National 
Water policy by the members of NWRC, a Working Group under the 
chairmanship of Union Minister of Water Resources was constituted to 
examine the draft provisions. The Working Group has discussed this issue and 
after arriving at a near consensus, it has recommended to NWRC inter-alia a 
draft provision on setting up of RBOs without proposing the 
statutory/regulatory powers thereto.

SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal):   Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is 
reported in the Press that the Minister of Disinvestment, using the 
platform of CH...

SHRI JIBON ROY:    Sir, I will just add one sentence.    
He has 
categorised the trade unions as obstructionists and has called them as 
'weakening power'.   Immediately, a day after that, the coal workers have 
gone on a total strike. 
The massive success of coal workers' strike yesterday, has 
busted the claim made in Cll confabulations by the Union Minister of 
Disinvestment day before yesterday, holding trade unions as 
'obstructionists' and calling them as 'weakening power'. This is the biggest 
strike in the recent period, encompassing six lakh miners in the length and 
breadth of the country. The strike was total; and it will continue till 
tomorrow. I believe, hon. Ministers will, henceforth, restrain. 
It brings no happiness to workers when they go on strike. The 
vastness of the strike has vindicat ed the reality that the strike was 
spontaneous and workers have found this call as an instrument to 
demonstrate their anguish against the Government policy of privatisation and 
deprivation. Through this strike, t he coal workers demanded from the 
Government the immediate withdrawal  of coal denationalisation Bill 
introduced in Parliament. Coal workers have seen from their 150 years' 
experience that the private regime has not provided any schools, community 
development projects or healthcare system. The coal workers are now 
convinced that the denationalisation process will not only bring distress to 
labour, but it will also ruin the industry. 
It is a matter of shame and agony that coal workers have not 
been paid their earned wage arrears for the last six years. I would 
have been glad if the Government had responded to the sentiments of 
workers, which I understand are unattainable from the people who use 
employers' platforms against labour. However, I hope the Government 
will come to terms with the united trade union movement.

Proposal to raise water level of Mullapperiyar Dam 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerela): Sir, it is very reliably 
learnt that there is a strong move to raise the water level of 
Mullapperiyar Dam in Kerala from 136 feet, without considering the 
genuine reservation of the Government of Kerala. The proposal to 
raise the water level of the Dam will adversely affect the environment. 
The increase of water level tends to destroy the forest and wild life of 
the surroundings, especially the Tiger  Reserve Project of Periyar in 
Kerala. 
The Mullapperiyar Dam was constructed long back and the 
strength and capacity of the Dam is in doubt. The safety of the Dam is 
in danger. During the recent continuous monsoon, high leakage of 
water was found through the Dam, causing apprehension among the 
people. 
If anything happens to the Dam, the population of Idukki, 
Kottayam and Ernakulam District will be totally affected and they will 
be devastated. All-party Conference convened by the Chief Minister of 
Kerala has already appealed to the Go vernment of India not to raise 
the water level of Mullapperiyar Dam. 
Considering all these facts, it is urged that the water level of 
Mullapperiyar Dam shall not be raised at any cost. 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, I associate myself 
with what the hon. Member has said. 
Release of Postal Stamp and Coin 
in the memory of Maruthupandiars 
SHRIMATI S. G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, this is regarding 
the release of a postal stamp and a coin in the memory of 
Maruthupandiars on their 200 th death anniversary. Maruthupandiars 
were the erstwhile rulers of Sivagangai land in Tamil Nadu dunng the 
18* century. That period was called the 'The Golden Age of 
Sivaganga Kingdom'. According to the Indian history, the ruler had 
issued a proclamation against the British Rule in 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001]  
India which was called the Thiruchirapalli Proclamation' and which 
emphasised that the British rulers should quit India. Maruthu brothers 
organised a disciplined movement against the British Government. 
They collected various kings of south India and organised a rebellion. 
The British troops started war against the brave brothers on 
28th May, 1801. The Maruthu brothers carried out guerrilla attacks 
against them. The war did not end as per the expectations of the 
British rulers. Because of their brave fighting, the war went on for 150 
days. The Maruthu brothers contin ued guerrilla attacks against the 
British Army. A prize money was a nnounced by the British Army for 
giving information about Maruthu brothers. It worked out. The Maruthu

THE NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION 
AND RESEARCH (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILISERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE):   Sir, I 
move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the National Institute of 
Pharmaceutical Education and Research Act, 1988, 
be taken into consideration." 
Sir, the Act was passed in 1988. The idea was to take over 
the management and assets and liabili ties of what is popularly known 
as NIPER. In the NIPER, there is a Board of Governors, and Section 4 
(3) (o) provides for nomination of Members - two Members from the 
Lok Sabha and one Member from t he Rajya Sabha - by the Speaker 
of the Lok Sabha and by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Now, sub-
section (4) of Section (4) provides for the tenure of office of other 
Governors, which is a fixed tenure of three years. But, so far as 
Members of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha are concerned, there 
is no tenure fixed. So, this amendment seeks to introduce a proviso to 
sub-section (4), under which the tenure will be fixed in the event of a 
Member of the Lok Sabha or of the Rajya Sabha becoming a Minister 
or a Minister of State or a Deputy Minister or the Deputy Chairman of 
the Rajya Sabha; in which case, he automatically ceases to be a 
member of the Board of Governors.  That is the proviso which is 
sought to be introduced. This Bill is merely for removing the anomaly 
and providing specifically for the t enure of office of members of the 
Board. 
The question was proposed.
